sketches.title: The Animal’s Apology Tour
sketches.premise: An animal is loose in town and keeps causing trouble. You build one apology from the animal, adding the next sentence each turn; make it sound sincere while quietly making the speaker look worse.
sketches.criterion: A sentence HOLDS if it follows the facts already stated, keeps the apology aimed at the same incident, and moves it one honest step forward; a skipped cause, a sudden ending, a contradiction, or an undo of an admitted fact BREAKS it.
sketches.move_shape: Add exactly one sentence that follows the last one. Example: “I knocked over the bakery sign because the croissant smelled like freedom.” The joke is the animal accepting blame while making itself, or its handler, look like an idiot.
sketches.first_card: A raccoon has been caught inside the town’s mayoral office.

sketches.title: People v. The Animal
sketches.premise: An animal is loose in town, and the town is putting it on trial. Build one shared case file, taking turns adding the next piece of evidence; the case may be fair, but your job is to make the other side’s animal look guilty as hell.
sketches.criterion: A piece HOLDS if it follows the timeline and evidence already on the table and advances the same case; a missing link, a final verdict before the evidence is complete, or taking back accepted evidence BREAKS it.
sketches.move_shape: Add exactly one new evidence item that connects to the existing chain. Example: “A wet paw print was found on the bakery window.” Score comes from how badly the item embarrasses the animal or traps the other player’s theory.
sketches.first_card: A goat is accused of eating the town’s spring festival banner.

sketches.title: Breaking News, Somehow
sketches.premise: An animal is loose in town, and you are building one live news report as events unfold. Take turns adding the next update; keep the report moving while slipping in details that make the reporter, the town, or the other player look spectacularly unprepared.
sketches.criterion: An update HOLDS if it follows the same live event, preserves every confirmed fact, and gives the next believable development; a skipped change, a wrap-up before the chase ends, or reversing a confirmed fact BREAKS it.
sketches.move_shape: Add exactly one broadcast update. Example: “The llama has now entered the library, where it appears to be judging the romance section.” Score comes from the sharpest embarrassment that still fits the report.
sketches.first_card: A peacock has escaped during the morning bus rush.

sketches.title: The Very Bad Rescue Plan
sketches.premise: An animal is loose in town, and together you plan how to get it somewhere safe. Add one next action at a time; the plan must stay possible, but you may make the tools, adults, and other player look painfully useless.
sketches.criterion: An action HOLDS if it can follow from the current location, tools, animal behavior, and earlier actions and still advances the same rescue; a skipped action, declaring the rescue finished, or undoing a used tool BREAKS it.
sketches.move_shape: Add exactly one action in the rescue chain. Example: “We leave the sardines by the fountain, then hide behind the statue.” Score comes from the cost imposed on the other player: public shame, filthy work, a ridiculous prop, or a choice that exposes their bad idea.
sketches.first_card: A nervous pig is loose in the town swimming pool.

sketches.title: What the Town Heard
sketches.premise: An animal is loose in town, and one rumor about it spreads from person to person. Build one shared chain of hearsay, adding the next retelling each turn; stay linked to the first sighting while making the rumor more embarrassing and less trustworthy.
sketches.criterion: A retelling HOLDS if it comes from the previous speaker, preserves the facts that person could know, and changes the same rumor by one believable step; a skipped speaker, a final truth, or erasing an established claim BREAKS it.
sketches.move_shape: Add exactly one person’s retelling. Example: “The florist told the milkman that the bear stole roses for a date.” Score comes from the cruelest believable twist that makes the other player’s chosen witness or claim look foolish.
sketches.first_card: A swan is seen blocking the town hall steps.

sketches.title: Pin the Beast
sketches.premise: An animal is loose in town, and you are drawing its route across one shared map. Take turns adding the next connected stop; the route must remain possible, but you should send the animal through places that make the other player explain an increasingly awful mess.
sketches.criterion: A stop HOLDS if it connects to the last location, fits the animal’s movement and the town facts already named, and keeps the route unfinished; a jump with no route, naming the destination, or moving back by denying a marked stop BREAKS it.
sketches.move_shape: Name exactly one next connected place and one small result there. Example: “From the bus depot, it slips into the laundromat and steals a sock.” Score comes from the trouble or humiliation the stop forces on the other player’s next move.
sketches.first_card: A horse bolts from the fairground into the town center.
